docs.title: Open Data Framework (odf)
docs.text:
Open Data Framework (ODF) is a Python framework for building data applications — small services that read, transform, and serve data — without the usual boilerplate. You write your data model and logic as plain Python classes; the framework wires them together and runs them. This package, odf, is the toolbelt around that: a CLI to scaffold and run projects, a UI to see and drive what's running, an MCP server so AI tools can act on your project too, and a chat window to talk to it directly.

Looking for the core abstractions?

Entity, Repository, Component, Service, Task, Pipeline, Agent, Function, Context, Project, and Config all live in the sibling opendataframework package, which this one depends on. This site covers the CLI, UI, MCP server, and chat only.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install odf                # CLI + scaffolding only
pip install "odf[ui]"          # + UI dev server
pip install "odf[mcp]"         # + MCP server
pip install "odf[ui,chat]"     # + chat window (served by the UI)

odf run starts the UI by default, so most projects want at least odf[ui].

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
pip install "odf[ui]"odf init my-projectCreated 'default' project 'my-project' in /path/to/my-projectcd my-projectodf runUI running at http://127.0.0.1:4747

Open http://127.0.0.1:4747 and select the Items node, then View, to see its records. The scaffolded app/ package is where your own entities, repositories and tasks go.

docs.title: What's in the package
docs.text:
• CLI: odf init scaffolds a project from one of five templates, and odf run starts one, optionally with the UI, MCP server and chat.
  • Server: odf.server.Server wraps an opendataframework.Project and is what odf run boots under the hood. Use it directly to run a project from Python: embedded in a larger app, a test fixture, a notebook.
  • UI: the topology of every component, grouped by Layer, with its actions, a view of each repository's data (table, map, timeseries, image, video, audio, document), and labelling of that data for later pipelines.
  • MCP Server: the same actions as MCP tools, plus each agent, function and component's own tools, for any MCP-speaking client.
  • Chat: a chat window in the UI, backed by a local Ollama model, that acts on the project through the MCP tools.
from odf.server import Server

server = Server.from_config("config.toml")
server.start(ui=True, mcp=True, chat=True)
server.wait()  # blocks until Ctrl+C/SIGTERM

docs.title: Chat
docs.text:
An optional chat window in the UI, backed by a local Ollama model. It can act on the project by calling the same tools the MCP server (see MCP Server) exposes — start/stop services, execute tasks and pipelines, query repositories, inspect logs — so you can drive the project conversationally instead of clicking through the UI.

Like the UI and MCP server, chat is not a DI-managed Component — it is started directly by Server.start() and requires an optional extra.

docs.title: Enabling
docs.text:
pip install "odf[ui,mcp,chat]"

server = Server.from_config("config.toml")
server.start(ui=True, mcp=True, chat=True)

chat=True requires ui=True — the chat window is served by the topology UI, on the same host/port, not a separate server. Passing chat=True without ui=True raises ValueError.

mcp=True is optional but recommended: without it, chat still answers questions as a plain LLM, but has no tool-calling access to the project (no starting/stopping components, no running tasks).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Connection parameters for the local Ollama daemon come from [project.chat] in config — not from a start() kwarg, since these are the kind of per-environment values that belong in config.toml:

[project.chat]
model = "gpt-oss:20b"
ollama-host = "http://localhost:11434"
debug = false
Key Default Description model "gpt-oss" Ollama model name. Must already be pulled (ollama pull gpt-oss:20b). ollama-host "http://localhost:11434" URL of the running Ollama daemon (ollama serve). debug false Show tool-call/tool-result debug info inline in the chat window.

docs.title: How tool-calling works
docs.text: When mcp=True is also passed, Server.start() hands the chat engine a reference to the same FastMCP instance the MCP server serves over streamable HTTP (McpServer.mcp) — tool definitions and execution are shared in-process, not duplicated. On each turn, the model is offered the current tool list — the six fixed tools (list_components, query_repository, start_component, stop_component, execute_task for a task or pipeline, component_logs) plus, for every resolved component that exposes its own MCP tools (prefixed by its key, <namespace>.<name>.<tool>), that component's own tools, for every resolved @Agent its <key>.invoke tool, and for every resolved @Function its <key>.call tool; these are dynamic per project, so they aren't enumerated here by name. If the model requests a tool call, it's always executed and its result fed back to the model for a follow-up reply; the chat window additionally shows what was called and its result inline only when [project.chat]'s debug is true.

docs.title: Addressing a component with @
docs.text:
Mentioning a component's key, @<namespace>.<name>, anywhere in a message scopes that turn's tool access to just that component — its own exposed tools (for an @Agent, its <key>.invoke, and for an @Function, its <key>.call), its own repository data (if it's a Repository), and its own lifecycle actions (start_component/stop_component/execute_task/component_logs, forced to that component regardless of what the model passes) — instead of offering every tool in the project. This is useful once a project has several repositories/services: instead of the model guessing which repository a data question is about, @repository.users how many rows are there? scopes query_repository to just that repository's data, and @agent.librarian anything by Herbert? hands the question to the Librarian agent's agent.librarian.invoke, with the arguments the model fills in from the agent's schema. @function.load-data load data.csv does the same through function.load-data.call.

The key is the node id the topology graph uses, and the prefix of the component's own tools (e.g. a @Task class MetricsFetcher is addressed as @task.metrics-fetcher). Always writing the namespace keeps a mention unambiguous as a project grows: a @Task class Loader and an @Agent class Loader are @task.loader and @agent.loader. The chat input autocompletes the key as you type @, matching the name or class name too. A mention that doesn't match any resolved component's key, such as a bare @loader, is just left as plain text — the turn falls back to the full, unscoped tool set. A message can only address one component at a time — mentioning more than one distinct component's key in the same message rejects the turn with an inline error instead of guessing which one you meant.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. Install and run Ollama locally: ollama serve.
  2. Pull a tool-calling-capable model: ollama pull gpt-oss:20b.
  3. Start the project with chat=True (and mcp=True for tool access).

If the Ollama daemon is unreachable, the chat window shows an inline error rather than hanging.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
The odf command-line tool scaffolds new projects and runs existing ones. It is installed with the package; the ui extra adds the UI odf run starts by default:

pip install "odf[ui]"Installed 
$ odf --help

 Usage: odf [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

 Open Data Framework CLI.

Commands:
  init  Scaffold a new ODF project: a config.toml and an importable app package.
  run   Start a project: import its app package, load its config, and run until Ctrl+C.

docs.title: odf init
docs.text:
Scaffolds a new project — a config.toml and an importable app package that registers components via decorators (@Entity, @Component, @Repository, ...).

odf init [NAME] [--template/-t TEMPLATE]
  • NAME — optional. If given, creates and scaffolds a new subdirectory ./NAME. If omitted, scaffolds into the current directory. Either way, the target must not already contain files.
  • --template / -t — which starting layout to scaffold. Defaults to default.

No template needs a dependency of its own: each is built on opendataframework plus the Python standard library (sqlite3 for storage). Running one with the UI, as odf run does by default, needs the odf[ui] extra.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
Every template starts from default's layout (one Entity, one Repository, one sqlite3-backed Storage) and adds one thing on top. Each has its own page with the full folder layout and what gets registered:

Template Adds on top of default default — nothing; this is the starting point itself data-analytics An @Analytics @Task that aggregates repository data and writes a JSON report data-science A seed CSV and a notebook that loads it into the repository data-engineering A SeedItems → ExportItemsSummary Pipeline reading data/raw/ and writing data/processed/ research A RunExperiment Task that loads data/items.csv and writes results/summary.json, plus a write-up stub

data-science, data-engineering, and data-analytics all borrow folder names from cookiecutter-data-science, the most widely used Python data-science project template — each ODF template takes just the piece relevant to its usecase rather than the whole layout. data-science and data-engineering use its data/raw/ (source data, never edited in place) → data/processed/ (derived output) split, expressed here with ODF's own Task/Pipeline abstractions instead of a separate orchestration tool. data-analytics uses its reports/ folder instead, since analytics is consumption-oriented: it reads repository data and produces a report artifact rather than ingesting one. research follows "Good Enough Practices in Scientific Computing" (Wilson et al., 2017): a flat data/ for raw, read-only input, a results/ for everything generated, and a doc/ for the write-up — app/ plays the role of that layout's src/.

odf init my-pipeline --template data-engineeringCreated 'data-engineering' project 'my-pipeline' in /path/to/my-pipelineNext steps: cd my-pipeline odf run

docs.title: odf run
docs.text:
Starts an existing project: imports its app package (registering all decorated components as a side effect), loads its config, and runs until Ctrl+C.

odf run [CONFIG] [OPTIONS]

Run it from the project's root directory — the one containing config.toml and the app package, the same layout odf init produces.

Argument / Option Default Description CONFIG config.toml Path to a config file or a directory of config files (see Project) --app app Import name of the package that registers components — see Server for the same convention used when building a Server directly in Python --ui / --no-ui --ui Start the UI --ui-host, --ui-port 127.0.0.1, 4747 Interface/port for the UI --theme config's [ui] theme, or default UI theme (visual file-set) to serve. Built in: default, glitch, neo, emerald, onyx (see UI) --mcp / --no-mcp --no-mcp Start the MCP server --mcp-host, --mcp-port 127.0.0.1, 4748 Interface/port for the MCP server --chat / --no-chat --no-chat Add a chat window to the UI (requires --ui) 
$ odf run
UI running at http://127.0.0.1:4747
Press Ctrl+C to stop

When opendataframework or odf rejects the project at start-up, odf run prints the reason on one line and exits with status 1, without a traceback. When the error comes from a decorator, the line ends with the file and line of the decorated class:

$ odf run
Error: Repository expects a class registered with @Entity, got 'Item'. Decorate it with @Entity — or, if Item is the repository itself, pass its entity: @Repository(SomeEntity) (app/repositories.py:8)

An exception raised by the project's own code, such as a constructor or a setup(), is shown with its full traceback.

The UI (--ui, on by default) requires the odf[ui] extra (fastapi/uvicorn); pass --no-ui to run without it. --mcp requires odf[mcp] and --chat requires odf[chat].

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Small, focused odf projects demonstrating the CLI/MCP/UI-server surface that sits on top of opendataframework. These depend on opendataframework as a real package dependency, so this directory doubles as an integration check that the split works for external consumers.

# Example Concept(s) Docs 1 01-table-view A repository implementing no data_view() at all, so the UI falls back to the implicit default plain table. View 2 02-data-analytics The data-analytics template layout: a SummarizeReadings @Analytics @Task writing a JSON report to reports/. Task, Layer 3 03-data-science The data-science template layout: data/raw/ ingested via Project, then explored from notebooks/ through a Repository built standalone, outside the Context. Repository 4 04-data-engineering The data-engineering template layout: SeedReadings + ExportReadingsSummary @Tasks composed by a Pipeline into a raw-to-processed ETL flow. Its [ui.topology] config hides the Config and SQLite nodes. Task, Pipeline, Topology view config 5 05-research The research template layout: a single RunExperiment @Task loading data/ into a repository and writing results/summary.json, alongside a doc/notes.md lab-notebook stub. Task 6 06-location-view A repository implementing data_view() -> LocationView so the UI renders a map instead of a table. View 7 07-streaming-video-view A stream-only Webcam repository (data_view() -> StreamingVideoView) rendered as a live video player with a Start/Stop toggle. View 8 08-video-view A SecurityClips repository (data_view() -> VideoView) rendered as a grid of video cards, each previewing a frame of its clip and opening it in a player. View 9 09-streaming-audio-view A stream-only DispatchRadio repository (data_view() -> StreamingAudioView) rendered as a live audio player. View 10 10-audio-view A VoiceMemos repository (data_view() -> AudioView) rendered as a grid of audio cards, each showing its clip's waveform and opening it in a player. View 11 11-image-view A DeliveryPhotos repository (data_view() -> ImageView) rendered as a grid of thumbnails that open full size, where labelled boxes can be drawn on them. View 12 12-document-view An OrderReceipts repository (data_view() -> DocumentView) rendered as cards that open each record's document: a JSON tree, text, or a PDF. File receipts are named and typed by content_metadata(). View 13 13-timeseries-view An Orders repository (data_view() -> TimeseriesView) rendered as a line chart, one point per record, where time ranges and points can be labelled. View 14 14-chart A SalesByStore component implementing chart() -> str, a matplotlib-backed self-contained HTML chart the UI renders behind a View Chart button. Component 15 15-chart-plotly The same ChartProtocol contract as 14-chart, backed by Plotly instead of matplotlib for real hover tooltips. Component 16 16-mcp-chat odf.server.Server.start(ui=True, mcp=True, chat=True) — the same resolved Context exposed as MCP tools and driven by a local Ollama chat window. Chat 17 17-custom-icon A config.toml-registered .js file ([ui] icon-scripts) and [ui.colors] entries adding a "Lighthouse" icon and named color swatches to the topology UI's pickers — pre-applied to the Beacons node via a committed layout.json — plus a custom favicon, header logo, and brand name ([ui] favicon / [ui] logo / [ui] brand). UI 18 18-custom-mcp-tool A StockRoom component whose mcp_tools() adds a typed stock-room.low_stock tool next to the fixed MCP tools. MCP Server 19 19-agent A Librarian @Agent whose invoke(question, limit=3) takes arguments: called through context.call(), invoked from a form in the UI, and exposed as its own typed agent.librarian.invoke MCP tool. MCP Server, Chat 20 20-function Adopting plain functions with @Function: to_eur and store_total keep their signatures and still work when called directly, while context.call() injects their Rates/Orders dependencies and another function through Annotated. Each one gets a Call action in the UI and its own typed <key>.call MCP tool. MCP Server, Chat

Examples 2–5 mirror odf init --template <name>'s scaffolded layouts — each is runnable both as a plain script (python main.py) and via odf run (see each example's own README.md for specifics). Most "Docs" entries above refer to concept pages on the opendataframework docs site — Entity, Repository, Task, Pipeline, Layer, View, and Component are all core abstractions documented there, not here. The UI, MCP server and chat each have their own page here: UI, MCP Server, Chat.

docs.title: Running an example
docs.text:
Clone the repository, install odf with the UI (pip install "odf[ui]"; some examples need more, such as opencv-python or matplotlib, listed in their own README.md), then run from inside the example's own directory:

cd examples/01-table-viewodf runUI running at http://127.0.0.1:4747

Open the UI and look at Books — it renders as a plain table with no extra step needed. Examples 2–5 can also run as a plain script instead of the UI (python main.py) — see each example's own README.md for specifics.

docs.title: MCP Server
docs.text:
Exposes the same actions available in the UI (service start/stop, task/pipeline execution, agent invocation, function calls, log inspection, repository data queries) as MCP tools for any MCP-speaking client.

pip install "odf[mcp]"
odf run --mcp

server.start(mcp=True)
print(server.mcp_url)  # http://127.0.0.1:4748/mcp

The server speaks the streamable HTTP transport and binds to --mcp-host/--mcp-port (127.0.0.1:4748 by default).

docs.title: Connecting a client
docs.text:
Point the client at the URL odf run prints. For example, with Claude Code:

claude mcp add --transport http my-project http://127.0.0.1:4748/mcp

The chat window uses the same tools in-process, with no client to configure.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Each tool takes a component's key, <namespace>.<name>, as its key argument (start_component(key="service.postgres")), and list_components returns it as each entry's id.

Tool Arguments Does list_components — Lists every resolved component, repository, service, task, pipeline, agent and function: its id, type, layer and, for a service, whether it is running query_repository key, limit=50, offset=0, filters=None Returns {"records": [...], "total": n}, a page of a repository's records. filters maps field names to case-insensitive substrings; limit is capped at 500 start_component key Starts a @Service; a no-op if it is running stop_component key Stops a @Service; a no-op if it is stopped execute_task key Executes a @Task or @Pipeline and returns what execute() returns component_logs key, lines=50 Returns the last log entries of any component

On top of these six, a project adds its own tools, each prefixed by its key.

docs.title: Agents and functions
docs.text:
Each resolved @Agent becomes its own tool, <key>.invoke (agent.librarian.invoke). Its input schema is invoke()'s signature and its description is the first paragraph of the class docstring, so a client is told what the agent takes rather than guessing at a generic arguments object. The tool calls the agent through context.call(), which logs the call to the agent's log. list_components lists agents with the type agent. An argument that can't be passed by keyword (positional-only, *args, **kwargs) is left out of the schema. See examples/19-agent.

Each resolved @Function becomes its own tool the same way, <key>.call (function.load-data.call). Its input schema is the function's signature, less the parameters the Context injects, and its description is the first paragraph of the function's docstring. list_components lists functions with the type function, and gives every entry a verb, invoke or call, when it has one of these tools. See examples/20-function.

docs.title: A component's own tools
docs.text:
Any resolved component can contribute its own tools by implementing opendataframework.component.McpToolsProtocol's mcp_tools(). They are prefixed by the component's key, so a @Component class StockRoom's low_stock tool is component.stock-room.low_stock. Two tools with the same full name raise a ValueError at start.

An McpTool needs a non-empty description and a fully typed handler: every parameter annotated, a return annotation (-> None counts), no *args/**kwargs, a method or function rather than a lambda, and no from __future__ import annotations in its module. The MCP server passes the description and the handler's signature to the client as the tool's description and input schema, which is all a model sees of the tool. opendataframework raises when a tool doesn't meet this, and odf run reports it as a start-up error. See examples/18-custom-mcp-tool.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• UI: onyx theme, a monochrome graphite take on Material Design 3, in both light and dark mode. Select it with odf run --theme onyx or [ui] theme = "onyx" in config.toml. See CLI.

  • UI: 51 more built-in topology icons, and an icon picker split into group tabs: Defaults, Devices, Buildings, Charts, Research, ML and Shop. Icons added through [ui] icon-scripts are listed under Custom, or under the group named by the optional group in ODF.registerIcon(key, draw, meta). The helpers the built-in icons are drawn with are available to custom icon scripts as ODF.iconKit.

  • UI: selecting a thumbnail in the image view opens that image full size, with the record's other fields as a caption, previous/next buttons (or the arrow keys), and the close button in the corner or Esc to return to the grid. Images are now served with the media type detected from their bytes (JPEG, PNG, GIF, WebP, BMP, TIFF, AVIF, HEIC) instead of always image/jpeg, and an image the browser can't decode, such as HEIC outside Safari, is labelled with its type instead of showing a broken-image icon.

  • UI: labelled boxes can be drawn on an open image in the image view. Pick Draw a box in the tool rail at the top left of the image, drag to draw a box and type its label, or pick one already used from the list under the input; select a box to delete it, or select its label to change it. A box inside a larger one stays on top, so it can still be selected. With Place a fixed-size box picked in the rail, every new box takes the width and height set beside it, in image pixels, for algorithms that need boxes of one size: click or drag to place one centred on the pointer, kept whole inside the image. A label no box uses any more is dropped from the list. Boxes are saved to annotations.json, or the file named by [project] annotations-file in config.toml, as pixel coordinates with each image's size and an ordered label list per repository, for a later pipeline to read with json.load. The 11-image-view example describes the format. [ui] annotations = false in config.toml turns annotating off.
  • UI: the video and audio views list their records as cards, like the image view: a video card previews a frame of its clip, an audio card its waveform (for clips up to 10 MB), both with the clip's length. Selecting a card opens the clip in a player and starts it, with the record's other fields as a caption, previous/next buttons, and the close button in the corner or Esc to return to the grid. Clips are now served with the media type detected from their bytes (MP4, QuickTime, WebM, Ogg, AVI, WAV, MP3, AAC, FLAC) instead of always video/mp4 or audio/wav, and with Range requests honored, so a clip can be seeked and plays in Safari. A clip the browser can't decode is labelled with its type.
  • UI: the document view lists its records as cards, like the image view, each previewing the start of its document. Selecting a card opens the document, with the record's other fields as a caption, previous/next buttons (or the arrow keys), and the close button in the corner or Esc to return to the grid. A DocumentView field can now hold a file as well as a JSON-shaped value: bytes are shown as a PDF (drawn by pdf.js, loaded from a CDN when first needed) or as text, detected from their content, and a str as text, while a dict or list is still a collapsible tree. Text that parses as JSON, such as a .json file, is a tree as well, and text that reads as Markdown is rendered, each with a button to switch to its source and back. Bytes of any other type are labelled with that type and can be downloaded. The 12-document-view example shows each kind.
  • UI: an open document in the document view can be labelled. With Label text picked in the tool rail, select text to label that span of it, or with Draw a box drag on a PDF page to draw a labelled box, as on an image; select a span or a box to delete it, or select its label to change it. Spans are drawn on text as it is written, so Label text shows a Markdown or JSON document as its source, and spans don't overlap. An image or document opens on the Select tool, which adds nothing and leaves selected text to be copied; the tool picked is remembered in the browser, and V, B, F and T pick one from the keyboard. A dict or list document takes no labels. They are saved to the same annotations.json as image boxes: a span as its start and end in the text, counted in characters as Python indexes a str, with the text it covers, and a page box in PDF points with its page number and the page's size. The 12-document-view example describes the format. [ui] annotations = false in config.toml turns annotating off.
  • UI: time ranges and points can be labelled on the chart of the timeseries view, for the simple cases a one-off script would otherwise be written for, such as a stretch to train on or leave out, an event, or a bad reading. Pick Label a range (R) beside the legend and drag across the chart, or Label a point (P) and click to mark the nearest record, then type a label or pick one already used; select a mark to delete it, or select its label to change it. A mark covers every series and ranges may overlap. They are saved to the same annotations.json as image boxes, as one list per repository: a range as its start and end in the timestamp field's own units, and a point as its record's timestamp and key. The 13-timeseries-view example describes the format. [ui] annotations = false in config.toml turns annotating off.
  • UI: time ranges and points can be labelled on a clip open in the video and audio views, for marking its segments and events, such as speech, an action or an onset. A timeline under the player spans the clip, with its waveform for audio and a line where it is playing. Pick Label a range (R) in the tool rail and drag on the timeline, or Label a point (P) and click it, then type a label or pick one already used. M marks where the clip is playing instead, which is finer on a long clip: a point, or one end of a range and then the other. Select a mark to delete it, or select its label to change it; a click elsewhere on the timeline seeks the clip there. Marks are saved to the same annotations.json, per record, in seconds from the start of the clip with the clip's length beside them. The 10-audio-view example describes the format. [ui] annotations = false in config.toml turns annotating off.
  • UI: labelled regions can be drawn on the map of the location view, for "everything inside this area", such as a region of interest, a geofence or a split by area. Pick Draw a region (B) at the top right of the map, drag out a rectangle and type its label or pick one already used. With Select (V) the map moves as before: select a region to delete it, or select its label to change it. A region inside a larger one stays on top. Regions are saved to the same annotations.json, as one list per repository, each as its south, west, north and east bounds in degrees. The 06-location-view example describes the format. [ui] annotations = false in config.toml turns annotating off.
  • UI: a record can be given a class, for simple classification such as good or bad, relevant or not. Under an image, document, video or audio clip open from its grid there is a row of the repository's classes: select one, or press its number (1 to 9), to give it to the open record, select + to add a class, and select the record's own class to take it away. The grid shows each record's class on its card. The table view has a class column with the same choice per row. A record has one class, and a class no record has any more is dropped from the list. Classes are saved to the same annotations.json, apart from box, span and range labels, as a map from record key to class with the list of classes in use. The 11-image-view example describes the format. [ui] annotations = false in config.toml turns it off.
  • Agents: @Agent classes (new in opendataframework 0.3.0) appear in the topology as agent nodes, with their own default icon and color, an entry in the type legend under the canvas, an Agents count in the header, and an agents list in [ui.topology]. A node's Invoke action opens a form built from the agent's invoke() arguments and shows the result. Over MCP each agent is its own tool, <key>.invoke (agent.librarian.invoke), with invoke()'s signature as its input schema, and @agent.librarian in the chat keeps that tool available for the message. Every call goes through context.call(), so it is logged to the agent's log. See the 19-agent example.
  • Functions: @Function functions (new in opendataframework 0.3.0) appear in the topology as function nodes, with their own default icon and color, an entry in the type legend under the canvas, and a Functions count in the header. They are linked to the components injected into them and to the classes and functions that ask for them through Annotated[Callable[...], func]. A functions list in [ui.topology] filters them. A node's Call action opens the same form as an agent's Invoke, with one field per argument the function takes beyond its injected ones, and calls it through context.call(). Over MCP each function is its own tool, <key>.call (function.load-data.call), with the same arguments as its input schema, and @function.load-data in the chat keeps that tool available for the message. list_components lists functions, with a verb on every entry that has such a tool. The logs of their calls are served at /api/functions/{name}/logs and by component_logs. See the 20-function example.
  • View: a repository implementing content_metadata(entity) (ContentMetadata, new in opendataframework 0.3.0) names and types its records' content in the image, video, audio and document views. A declared content_type is served instead of the type detected from the bytes when it fits the view, and a document is still only ever a PDF, plain text or a download. A declared filename labels the record's card and its caption when open, is sent as Content-Disposition, and names the file saved by the new Download action in the open record's tool rail. A text document declared as Markdown (text/markdown or a .md name) is rendered, and one declared as anything else is shown as written, instead of either being judged by its text. The records payload carries both under a $content key. See the 12-document-view example.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Deps: requires opendataframework >=0.3.0,<0.4.0. Upstream addresses every component by its <namespace>.<name> key and adds @Agent, @Function and ContentMetadata, which the entries above and below build on.
  • UI: the Activity and Chat buttons moved from the top-right corner of the map into the header bar, as icon buttons next to the theme toggle. They no longer cover a view's own controls, such as the table view's timeline dropdown and replay controls, and the button of the open drawer stays highlighted.
  • UI: the popup shown when selecting a component lists its actions as one list of full-width rows instead of buttons of different widths. The component's own actions, such as View, Start or Execute, come first, followed by Show Logs and Customize. Its type, layer and file are shown as labelled rows under the description.
  • CLI: odf run prints a project set-up error as one line instead of a traceback: a check in opendataframework or odf that rejects the project, such as @Repository on a class with no @Entity, an async def lifecycle method, a dependency declared twice, an McpTool without a typed handler or an unknown theme. When the error comes from a decorator, the line ends with the file and line of the decorated class. An error raised by the project's own code keeps its traceback, and a project that fails to start is stopped before odf run exits. Set-up errors that were reported as Invalid value now read Error. See CLI.
  • Keys (breaking): components are addressed by their opendataframework key, <namespace>.<name> (task.load-job, service.postgres), everywhere odf names one, so same-named classes in different namespaces no longer collide. A topology node's id is its key, with name and href alongside. The UI's HTTP API serves each execution type as its own collection by registered name, such as POST /api/tasks/load-job/execute and GET /api/agents/librarian/parameters, instead of everything under /api/components/{id}, and an action that doesn't apply to a kind answers 404. The MCP tools start_component, stop_component, execute_task, component_logs and query_repository take a key argument instead of name or repo_id, and a component's own tools are prefixed by its key (component.stock-room.low_stock). Chat addresses a component as @<namespace>.<name>. Saved positions, icons and colors in layout.json were keyed by the old ids, so the topology resets them once after upgrading. See UI, MCP Server and Chat.
  • Templates: config sections are named after each class's key, following opendataframework 0.3.0: odf init writes [component.sqlite] instead of [sqlite], and the data-analytics task reads [task.summarize-items]. The scaffolded SQLite storage is registered as @Component(name="sqlite"), so its key is component.sqlite rather than component.s-q-lite. The examples follow the same layout. A project scaffolded by an earlier version keeps working as it is. See Templates.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • Examples: 08-video-view seeds playable clips on Linux. It encoded them as H.264 only, which the opencv-python wheels for Linux can't write, so the clips were empty; it now falls back to VP8 (WebM) or MPEG-4 Part 2. See Examples.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• UI: selectable themes. odf run --theme or [ui] theme in config.toml picks one of default, glitch, neo or emerald; Server.start(theme=) does the same. An unknown theme is reported as a CLI parameter error. See CLI and Server.
  • UI: collapsible left sidebar with an icon tab rail. The collapsed state and the active tab persist per browser.
  • UI: [ui.topology] config controls what the topology shows. connections = false hides the links between components, config = false hides the Config node, and repositories/services/tasks/pipelines/components lists restrict which components of that kind are shown (a kind without a list shows all of its components). Links of hidden components are bridged so the remaining graph keeps its shape, and the layout is recomputed on the visible set. An unknown key or a value of the wrong type raises ValueError; a listed name that matches no component emits a warning. A saved node position that collides with another node moves the other node to the nearest free row in its column. See Server.
  • MCP: query_repository tool for paged/filtered access to a repository's data, using the same query pattern as the UI's data table.
  • MCP: components that expose mcp_tools() (new in opendataframework 0.2.0) get their tools registered as <kebab(ClassName)>.<tool-name>, alongside the built-in tools. A duplicate tool name within one component raises at construction.
  • Chat: @component-id addressing scopes a turn's tools to that component: its own mcp_tools(), query_repository for a Repository, and the lifecycle tools. An unrecognized handle falls back to the full tool set, and a message that mentions more than one component returns an inline error. The chat input offers @ autocomplete. See Chat.
  • Chat: [project.chat] debug config flag (default false). See Chat.
  • Examples: 18-custom-mcp-tool, a component exposing a parameterized MCP tool. 17-custom-icon now uses the neo theme. See Examples.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Deps: requires opendataframework >=0.2.0,<0.3.0. Upstream renamed ReplayProtocol.replay_field to field and now raises on Namespace name collisions instead of silently overwriting.
  • Chat: tool_call/tool_result events are only shown in the chat window when [project.chat] debug = true. They were previously always shown. Tool execution is unaffected.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • UI: the Customize popover now closes when a data, details, chart or logs view is opened. It previously stayed on top of the view.

docs.title: Server
docs.text: odf.server.Server wraps an opendataframework.Project and adds the optional UI, MCP server, and chat orchestration that need third-party dependencies. odf run (see CLI) is a thin wrapper around exactly this class — use Server directly when you want to boot a project from Python instead: embedded in a larger application, a test fixture, a notebook, or any process that isn't the odf CLI.

docs.title: A minimal app
docs.text:
Every Server is built around two things: a config.toml and an app package that registers components as a side effect of being imported — the same layout odf init scaffolds.

# config.toml
[project]
name = "my-project"

# app/entities.py
from dataclasses import dataclass

from opendataframework import Entity


@Entity
@dataclass
class Book:
    id: int | None
    title: str
    author: str

# app/repositories.py
from opendataframework import Repository, Storage

from app.entities import Book


@Storage
@Repository(Book)
class Books:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._books: list[Book] = []

# app/__init__.py
from app import entities, repositories

__all__ = ["entities", "repositories"]

# main.py
from odf.server import Server

server = Server.from_config("config.toml")
server.start(ui=True)

print(f"UI running at {server.ui_url}")
print("Press Ctrl+C to stop")

server.wait()

$ python main.py
UI running at http://127.0.0.1:4747
Press Ctrl+C to stop

This is exactly what examples/01-table-view does — see Examples for more.

docs.title: The app module
docs.text:
Decorator registration (@Entity, @Repository, @Component, @Service, @Task, @Pipeline, ...) is a side effect of the class definition actually executing — nothing registers until the module that defines it gets imported. Server.start() handles this for you: before resolving the Context, it imports one entry-point module, controlled by app_module.

app_module Behavior "app" (default) Import a module/package named app from the current working directory before resolving. Matches odf run's --app default — a project laid out by odf init needs nothing extra passed. A missing app module is not an error; it's silently ignored, since components may already be registered some other way. "my_pkg" Import a differently named module/package instead — pass whatever name your entry point actually has. None Skip the import entirely. Use this if you've already imported your components yourself (e.g. earlier in the same script) and don't want start() to attempt anything on your behalf.

The one file that actually gets imported (app, by default) doesn't need to define components itself — it just needs to import whatever does, the way app/__init__.py above imports entities/repositories. Anything reachable transitively from that one import registers.

If, after resolving, zero application components were registered — no matter why (wrong app_module, a module that imports but forgot to decorate anything, or app_module=None with nothing registered elsewhere) — start() emits a UserWarning rather than silently booting an empty project:

>>> server.start()
<stdin>:1: UserWarning: Server.start() resolved zero application
components — no module named 'app' could be imported to register them
(or app_module=None was passed). Pass app_module= to point at the
package that defines your @Entity/@Repository/@Component classes, or
import it yourself before calling start().

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
server = Server.from_config("config.toml")  # or Server.from_dict({...}), or Server(...)

server.start(ui=True, mcp=False, chat=False)  # non-blocking — returns immediately
server.wait()  # blocks until Ctrl+C/SIGTERM or stop()
  • start(ui=, ui_host=, ui_port=, theme=, mcp=, mcp_host=, mcp_port=, chat=, app_module=) resolves the Context (importing app_module first, see above), then optionally starts the MCP server and UI — each backgrounded on its own daemon thread, like any Service. Always returns immediately, whether or not ui=/mcp= were passed, so you can do something with server.ui_url/server.mcp_url before ceding control of the process.
  • wait() blocks the calling thread until interrupted by Ctrl+C (SIGINT) or SIGTERM (the signal process managers/containers send to request a clean shutdown), or until another thread calls stop() directly — then stops the server itself. Call it once you're done with any setup that has to happen between start() returning and blocking (printing URLs, as above); skip it entirely if you're embedding Server in something that manages its own process lifecycle.
  • run(**same kwargs as start()) is start(...) followed by wait() in one call — the one-liner for a script whose only job is to keep a foreground server alive:
Server.from_config("config.toml").run(ui=True)
  • stop() tears down the UI, MCP server, and the underlying Project, in that order. Safe to call even if start() was never called, and safe to call more than once.
  • Context manager — with Server.from_config(...) as server: calls start()/stop() (not wait() — the block still runs immediately; add your own server.wait() inside if you want it to block too).

docs.title: Reading the resolved graph
docs.text:
server.context.get(Books).all()  # typed access to a resolved instance
server.context.instances  # {cls: instance} for everything resolved
server.config  # the raw config dict

server.context and server.config are available both before and after start() — see the sibling opendataframework docs for what Context/Config expose in full.

docs.title: UI
docs.text:
A small FastAPI dev server (backgrounded, like any Service) that visualizes the resolved object graph — every Component/Service/ Repository, grouped by Layer, with lifecycle actions (start/stop/ execute) available from the UI. Grid positions persist across reloads. The left sidebar collapses to an icon rail to give the canvas more room; its collapsed/expanded state is remembered per browser.

pip install "odf[ui]"
odf run                # the UI is on by default

server.start(ui=True)
print(server.ui_url)  # http://127.0.0.1:4747

The home page embeds a live, static snapshot of the UI.

docs.title: Topology
docs.text:
Each node is identified by its opendataframework key, <namespace>.<name> (task.load-job, agent.librarian), so two classes with the same name in different namespaces stay apart.

Dragging a node to a new cell, changing its icon or color, and adding cells to the grid are saved to layout.json in the working directory, or the file named by [project] layout-file. Commit it to share a layout. Icons are stored by key, so a node whose icon key no longer exists falls back to its type's default.

docs.title: Choosing what the topology shows
docs.text:
By default the topology shows every component and every connection between them. The [ui.topology] table in config narrows that:

[ui.topology]
connections = false                  # default true: draw links between components
config = false                       # default true: show the Config node
repositories = ["readings"]          # only these repositories
tasks = ["seed-readings"]            # only these tasks
agents = []                          # no agents
functions = ["load-data"]            # only these functions
components = []                      # no plain components (e.g. a Storage component)

repositories, services, tasks, pipelines, agents, functions and components each take registered names, the name part of each key (seed-readings for task.seed-readings), in any casing. A kind without a list shows all of its components; a kind with a list shows only the listed ones, and an empty list hides the kind. A component added later to a kind that has a list stays hidden until it is added to that list. A Storage component counts as a plain component.

When a component is hidden, the components that depend on it are linked to whatever it depends on, so the remaining graph keeps its shape. The remaining nodes are laid out again without gaps. A node whose saved grid position is taken by another node moves to the nearest free row in its column; those adjustments are not written to the layout file. Hidden components keep running and stay available through MCP and chat; only the topology view changes. Unknown keys and values of the wrong type raise a ValueError when the UI starts, and a listed name that matches no component produces a warning. See examples/04-data-engineering.

docs.title: Data views
docs.text:
Repositories can declare a data_view() to pick how their data renders (table, map, timeseries, image, video, audio, document, streaming video/audio) instead of the default table. The view types themselves are documented upstream in View; the Examples page has one example per view (01, 06–13).

A repository whose view shows content (an image, video, audio or document view) can also implement content_metadata(entity) to name and type each record's content. A declared content_type is served instead of the type worked out from the bytes, as long as it fits the view: an image view only takes an image type, never SVG, and a document is still only ever served as a PDF, plain text or a download. A declared filename labels the record's card and its caption, is sent as Content-Disposition, and names the file the Download action saves. A text document declared as Markdown, by a text/markdown type or a .md name, is rendered, and one declared as anything else is shown as written. Records list it, under a $content key, so the UI has it without a request per record. See examples/12-document-view.

A component implementing details() gets a details panel, and one implementing chart() a View Chart button (see examples/14-chart).

docs.title: Labelling data
docs.text:
The views can label records for the simple cases a one-off script would otherwise be written for: training data, events, regions of interest, a good/bad split. Labels are picked from a tool rail (or the keyboard), typed once and then picked from a list, and a label no mark uses any more is dropped.

View What can be labelled Keys Format described in Image Boxes, freely drawn or of one fixed size B box, F fixed-size box 11-image-view Document Text spans, and boxes on a PDF page T text, B box 12-document-view Video, audio Time ranges and points on the clip's timeline R range, P point, M mark at the playhead 10-audio-view Timeseries Time ranges and points on the chart R range, P point 13-timeseries-view Location Rectangular regions on the map B region 06-location-view

In every view V picks the Select tool, which adds nothing: it moves the map, or leaves text to be selected and copied. Select a mark to delete it, or its label to change it.

A record can also be given one class: from the row of classes under an open image, document or clip (1 to 9 pick one), or from the table view's class column. See 11-image-view.

Everything is saved to annotations.json in the working directory, or the file named by [project] annotations-file, as one block per repository, keyed by its registered name. The file is plain JSON, so a later pipeline reads it with json.load and no odf import. Images use pixel coordinates with the image's size, document spans character offsets into the text, PDF boxes points with the page's size, clips seconds with the clip's length, timeseries the timestamp field's own units, and map regions degrees. [ui] annotations = false turns labelling off.

docs.title: Arguments: Invoke and Call
docs.text: An @Agent's node has an Invoke action, and an @Function's node a Call action. Each opens a form with one field per argument, prefilled with the defaults, and shows the result under it. An agent's arguments are those of its invoke(). A function's are its own, less the parameters the Context injects. A str, number or bool argument gets an input of that kind, and any other type a JSON field. Values are converted to the annotated types before context.call() makes the call, and a value that doesn't fit is reported under the form without making it. See examples/19-agent and examples/20-function.

docs.title: Themes, icons and branding
docs.text:
The UI ships five themes: default, glitch, neo, emerald and onyx. Pick one with odf run --theme <name>, server.start(theme=...), or [ui] theme in config. A theme only restyles the UI; markup and behavior are the same in every theme. An unknown theme name raises a ValueError at start.

A node's icon and color can be changed from its "Customize" popover, which lists the built-in isometric icons by group (devices, buildings, charts, research, ML, shop). Icons and colors can be extended beyond the built-in set via [ui] icon-scripts / [ui.colors] in config, or by packages registering into odf.ui.extensions. The favicon, header logo, and "ODF" brand label can likewise be overridden with [ui] favicon / [ui] logo / [ui] brand. See examples/17-custom-icon.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Every key odf reads from config.toml:

Key Default Description [ui] theme "default" UI theme; --theme / theme= override it [ui] icon-scripts [] .js files registering extra icons [ui.colors] — Named color swatches added to the color picker [ui] favicon, [ui] logo built-in Image files replacing the favicon and header logo [ui] brand "ODF" Brand label in the header [ui] annotations true Allow labelling data in the views [ui.topology] show everything What the topology shows (see above) [project] layout-file "layout.json" Where node positions, icons and colors are saved [project] annotations-file "annotations.json" Where labels and classes are saved [project.chat] — Chat model and Ollama host (see Chat)

docs.title: HTTP API
docs.text:
The UI's HTTP API serves each execution type as its own collection, by registered name:

Route For GET /api/{collection}/{name}/logs any component (components, repositories, services, tasks, pipelines, agents, functions) GET /api/{collection}/{name}/details, .../chart a component implementing details() / chart() POST /api/services/{name}/start, .../stop a @Service POST /api/tasks/{name}/execute, /api/pipelines/{name}/execute a @Task / @Pipeline GET /api/agents/{name}/parameters, POST .../invoke an @Agent GET /api/functions/{name}/parameters, POST .../call an @Function /api/repositories/{name}/records, .../stream, ... a @Repository's data

The collection comes from the execution type, not the key's namespace: a @Task registered as loader is /api/tasks/loader, whatever its key. An action that doesn't apply to a kind has no route, so it answers 404.

docs.title: data-analytics template
docs.text:
odf init my-project --template data-analytics

default (Item/Items/SQLite) plus one @Analytics @Task: SummarizeItems, which aggregates the repository into a JSON report. Analytics is consumption-oriented — it reads repository data and produces a report artifact, rather than ingesting one the way data-engineering/research do.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
my-project/
├── config.toml
├── app/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── analytics.py      # SummarizeItems (@Analytics @Task)
│   ├── entities.py       # Item
│   ├── repositories.py   # Items(SQLite)
│   └── storages.py       # SQLite
└── reports/               # starts empty — SummarizeItems writes here

docs.title: What's added
docs.text:
# app/analytics.py
@Analytics
@Task
class SummarizeItems:
    def execute(self) -> dict:
        all_items = self.items.all()
        summary = {
            "item_count": len(all_items),
            "total_quantity": sum(item.quantity for item in all_items),
        }
        ...  # written to reports/summary.json
        return summary

The report path comes from [task.summarize-items] report-path in config (default "reports/summary.json"). @Analytics marks it for the Layer the UI groups analytics-style tasks under; @Task is what makes it executable from the UI's Execute action or the MCP execute_task tool.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
odf runUI running at http://127.0.0.1:4747

Trigger SummarizeItems from the UI (or execute_task over MCP) and check reports/summary.json.

docs.title: data-engineering template
docs.text:
odf init my-project --template data-engineering

default (Item/Items/SQLite) plus two @Tasks composed by a @Pipeline: SeedItems ingests data/raw/ into the repository, ExportItemsSummary aggregates it back out to data/processed/ — a raw-to-processed ETL flow expressed with ODF's own Task/Pipeline abstractions instead of a separate orchestration tool.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
my-project/
├── config.toml
├── app/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── entities.py       # Item
│   ├── storages.py       # SQLite
│   ├── repositories.py   # Items(SQLite)
│   ├── tasks.py          # SeedItems, ExportItemsSummary
│   └── pipelines.py      # SetupPipeline
└── data/
    ├── raw/
    │   └── items.csv      # source data — read, never edited in place
    └── processed/         # starts empty — ExportItemsSummary writes here

docs.title: What's added
docs.text:
# app/tasks.py
@Task
class SeedItems:
    def execute(self) -> int:
        if self.items.all():
            return 0  # dedup guard — skip if already seeded
        ...  # reads data/raw/items.csv, calls items.save(...) per row


@Task
class ExportItemsSummary:
    def execute(self) -> str: ...  # aggregates Items, writes data/processed/items_summary.json

# app/pipelines.py
@Pipeline
class SetupPipeline:
    def __init__(self, seed: SeedItems, export: ExportItemsSummary) -> None:
        self.seed = seed
        self.export = export

    def execute(self) -> None:
        self.seed.execute()
        self.export.execute()

SetupPipeline composes both tasks by declaring them as constructor dependencies — the Context resolves and injects them, the same way it would any other @Component.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
odf runUI running at http://127.0.0.1:4747

Trigger SetupPipeline from the UI (or execute_task over MCP), then check data/processed/items_summary.json.

docs.title: data-science template
docs.text:
odf init my-project --template data-science

default (Item/Items/SQLite), no app/ changes at all — just a seed CSV and a notebook that loads it into the repository outside the running Project, to show a Repository works standalone in a notebook kernel the same way it does DI-resolved inside one.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
my-project/
├── config.toml
├── app/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── entities.py       # Item
│   ├── repositories.py   # Items(SQLite)
│   └── storages.py       # SQLite
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   │   └── items.csv      # source data — read, never edited in place
│   └── processed/         # starts empty
└── notebooks/
    └── example.ipynb

docs.title: What's added
docs.text:
example.ipynb builds the same SQLite → Items dependency chain the Context would normally wire up for you, but by hand — since a notebook kernel runs outside the resolved object graph:

from opendataframework import Config

from app.entities import Item
from app.repositories import Items
from app.storages import SQLite

config = Config({"component": {"sqlite": {"path": "../app.db"}}})
sqlite = SQLite(config)
items = Items(sqlite)

Then it reads data/raw/items.csv and calls items.save(...) per row — the same ingestion a real Task would do, just exploratory. Anything derived (cleaned, joined, aggregated) belongs in data/processed/, never written back to raw/.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
jupyter notebook notebooks/example.ipynb

Or start the UI as usual (odf run) to browse Items once the notebook has seeded it.

docs.title: default template
docs.text:
odf init my-project

The bare starting point every other template builds on: one Entity, one Repository, one sqlite3-backed Storage. No dependencies beyond opendataframework and the Python standard library; odf run with its default UI needs the odf[ui] extra.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
my-project/
├── config.toml
└── app/
    ├── __init__.py
    ├── entities.py       # Item
    ├── repositories.py   # Items(SQLite)
    └── storages.py       # SQLite

docs.title: What's registered
docs.text:
• Item (app/entities.py) — an @Entity dataclass with id, name, quantity.
  • Items (app/repositories.py) — an @Storage @Repository(Item) backed by SQLite, exposing all()/get()/save()/delete().
  • SQLite (app/storages.py) — an @Storage @Component registered as sqlite (key component.sqlite) that opens the path from [component.sqlite] path in config (default "app.db") and creates the items table if it doesn't exist yet.
# config.toml
[project]
name = "my-project"

[component.sqlite]
path = "app.db"

app/__init__.py imports entities, repositories, and storages so their decorators register as a side effect — see Server for why that import matters.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
odf runUI running at http://127.0.0.1:4747

Open the UI — Items renders as a plain table with no extra step needed.

Every other template starts from exactly this layout and adds one thing on top — see the Templates comparison for data-analytics, data-science, data-engineering, and research.

docs.title: research template
docs.text:
odf init my-project --template research

default (Item/Items/SQLite) plus a single RunExperiment @Task and a write-up stub, following "Good Enough Practices in Scientific Computing" (Wilson et al., 2017): a flat data/ for raw, read-only input, a results/ for everything generated, and a doc/ for the write-up — app/ plays the role of that layout's src/.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
my-project/
├── config.toml
├── app/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── entities.py       # Item
│   ├── storages.py       # SQLite
│   ├── repositories.py   # Items(SQLite)
│   └── experiments.py    # RunExperiment
├── data/
│   └── items.csv          # source data — read, never edited in place
├── results/                # starts empty — RunExperiment writes here
└── doc/
    └── notes.md            # hypothesis / method / results stub

docs.title: What's added
docs.text:
# app/experiments.py
@Task
class RunExperiment:
    def execute(self) -> dict:
        if not self.items.all():
            ...  # seeds data/items.csv into Items, first run only

        all_items = self.items.all()
        summary = {
            "item_count": len(all_items),
            "total_quantity": sum(item.quantity for item in all_items),
        }
        ...  # written to results/summary.json
        return summary

doc/notes.md is a lab-notebook stub — hypothesis, method, results, notes — pre-filled with a pointer back to RunExperiment so the write-up and the code that produces its numbers stay next to each other.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
odf runUI running at http://127.0.0.1:4747

Trigger RunExperiment from the UI (or execute_task over MCP), then check results/summary.json and fill in doc/notes.md.
